tldr: This paper presents a framework that directly generates humanoid whole-body motions from monocular human videos and post-trains the generator with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) using tracking success/failure feedback from downstream policies, achieving high-quality and physically executable control.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of ViT-H. On the left, a diffusion model directly generates reference motions for the G1 from video features. In the center, the generator is post-trained with DPO using tracking results from both a deployable tracker and a privileged tracker. On the right, the framework supports both offline control and real-time teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency using an autoregressive variant.
overview:
Monocular human video is a treasure trove of motion data that is far more diverse and scalable than motion capture. However, existing methods that try to control humanoid robots from video have relied on a three-stage pipeline: reconstruct the human 3D pose from video, retarget it to the robot's morphology, and then track the trajectory with a control policy. This structure has a major flaw: intermediate errors snowball across stages, often producing motions that look natural for humans but are physically impossible for a robot to execute.

To address this, the authors propose ViT-H, a framework that completely bypasses intermediate human reconstruction and retargeting. Instead, it generates reference trajectories directly for the robot (Unitree G1) from monocular video using a diffusion model. Even cleverer is the post-training strategy: it scores whether a downstream control policy (tracker) succeeded in tracking the generated motion, and post-trains the generator using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Because tracking outcomes serve as rewards, the model can self-improve and discover "motions the robot can actually execute" even from uncurated internet videos without ground-truth 3D motion.

Experiments in simulation and on the real Unitree G1 demonstrate motion quality and tracking success rates that significantly outperform conventional pipelines. An autoregressive variant enables real-time teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency, and the framework exhibits favorable scaling behavior as model capacity and data scale increase.
contributions: Proposed ViT-H, a diffusion-based framework that generates humanoid joint-space motions directly from monocular video without human 3D reconstruction or retargeting.

Introduced a DPO post-training method that uses execution feedback from downstream whole-body tracking policies, enabling the generator to learn executable motions even from videos lacking ground-truth 3D labels.
Built an autoregressive model conditioned on past motion history for chunked generation, achieving real-time hardware teleoperation from a single monocular RGB camera with sub-400 ms latency.
Demonstrated significant improvements over conventional pipelines on the physical Unitree G1 and in simulation, establishing favorable scaling laws across model sizes and data scales.

sections.heading: Breaking through the two limits of conventional video-to-robot pipelines
sections.summary: Large collections of human video are a promising source for robot learning, but traditional "reconstruct-retarget-track" pipelines suffer from error accumulation and a lack of downstream feedback. ViT-H breaks through this barrier by generating reference motions directly from video and feeding execution feedback back into the generator.
sections.details:
Monocular videos across the web capture a diversity of whole-body behaviors that motion capture alone cannot match. Yet, most existing systems that teach robots from these videos rely on a three-stage pipeline: (1) reconstruct human 3D pose from video, (2) retarget the pose to humanoid morphology by recomputing joint angles and positions, and (3) track the resulting trajectory with a control policy.

This pipeline faces two critical system-level bottlenecks. The first is error accumulation. Human reconstruction models have no awareness of robot mass or joint limits, and downstream retargeting cannot look back at visual cues lost during reconstruction. The second is the inability to optimize executability end-to-end. Even when reconstruction and retargeting succeed visually, the resulting trajectories often cause the robot to tumble when handed over to a tracking policy.

This paper proposes ViT-H to flip the paradigm. It builds a diffusion model that maps directly from video into the motion space of the target robot (here, the 29-DoF Unitree G1). The generated motion is then executed by a tracking policy, which scores how smoothly and stably it could follow the trajectory. These scores guide post-training via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), closing the loop between generation and control.

sections.heading: Connecting 3D human reconstruction, retargeting, and control
sections.summary: While monocular 3D reconstruction and humanoid retargeting have advanced independently, keeping them decoupled fails to guarantee downstream executability. ViT-H unifies both steps into a single generative model and optimizes directly using motion-tracking feedback, setting it apart from prior work.
sections.details:
### Human Motion Reconstruction from Monocular Video
Techniques that recover 3D human pose from video using parametric body models (such as SMPL-X) have advanced rapidly, including methods that disentangle camera motion from body translation to estimate global trajectories. However, these focus solely on human bodies and ignore robot-specific dynamics and joint limits.

### Motion Retargeting from Human to Humanoid
Retargeting techniques that map human kinematics to robot joint angles (e.g., GMR and PHUMA) have also matured. Still, because they run as standalone modules in the inference pipeline, they inevitably inherit upstream reconstruction errors. ViT-H eliminates this conversion step entirely during inference.

### Humanoid Motion Generation and Whole-Body Tracking
Modern whole-body tracking policies (such as SONIC) provide a strong foundation capable of following diverse reference motions. On the generative side, while prior work has explored generating motions from text, very few efforts feed tracking feedback back into the generator's training. Some related works utilize physics simulation feedback, but they still optimize within the human motion space before retargeting. ViT-H instead optimizes directly within the robot's motion space using feedback from the tracker.

sections.heading: Closing the loop: diffusion models and DPO post-training
sections.summary: ViT-H builds a diffusion model that directly predicts whole-body joint poses and global trajectories from video features, constructs DPO preference pairs evaluated by both standard and privileged trackers, and supports low-latency real-time teleoperation via an autoregressive extension.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Video-to-Humanoid Motion Generation
The model takes relative camera poses, human 2D bounding boxes, 2D keypoints, and image features extracted from video as input. The output robot motion $\mathbf{X}$ comprises root translational velocity, root rotation in both camera and gravity frames, and 6D rotation representations for each joint.
The generator $\pi_{\text{gen}}$ uses a DDPM-based diffusion model parameterized to directly predict clean motion ($\mathbf{X}_0$-prediction). Forward kinematics (FK) yields joint positions and mesh vertices, which are supervised during pre-training using auxiliary losses including global translation loss, foot/hand contact stillness loss, and 2D reprojection loss.

### 3.2 DPO Post-Training with Motion Tracking Feedback
This is the core insight of the work. The authors fine-tune the pre-trained SONIC tracker into two versions: a deployable standard tracker $\pi_{\text{track}}$, and a privileged tracker $\pi_{\text{track}}^{\text{priv}}$ that observes global tracking offsets relative to the reference motion.
For each video, the generator samples multiple candidate motions, which are executed by both trackers. A reward is computed based on local pose error, global trajectory error, and episode survival (whether the robot avoided falling). Pairing trajectories with large reward gaps yields preference pairs: a preferred motion $\mathbf{X}^+$ that the tracker followed well, and a dispreferred motion $\mathbf{X}^-$ where it struggled. These pairs are used to fine-tune the generator using DPO adapted for diffusion models. Because no ground-truth 3D data is required, the model can leverage unlabeled in-the-wild videos to learn executable behaviors.

### 3.3 Autoregressive Generation for Teleoperation
Beyond batch offline generation over entire videos, the authors introduce an autoregressive generator $\pi_{\text{gen}}^{\text{ar}}$ to handle streaming video in real time. It generates motion in fixed-length chunks of $T$ frames, inpainting the first $L$ frames of the next chunk with the tail of the preceding chunk to ensure smooth transitions.

sections.heading: Outperforming conventional pipelines: higher success and clear scaling laws
sections.summary: Simulated and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms traditional reconstruction-retargeting pipelines in both motion quality and tracking success. DPO post-training substantially boosts success on challenging internet videos and generalizes to unseen trackers.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Comparison with Conventional Pipelines
Evaluation was conducted on benchmark datasets with 3D ground truth (EMDB and RICH) as well as an in-the-wild internet video dataset featuring dynamic dancing and gymnastics. Baselines combined state-of-the-art human reconstruction methods (GVHMR, GEM) with a retargeting pipeline (GMR).
In motion quality evaluations (Table 1), ViT-H (offline) outperformed baselines across mean per-joint position error (MPJPE), jitter, and self-penetration. In MuJoCo tracking experiments evaluating executability (Table 2), tracking success rates improved dramatically. On challenging internet videos where conventional pipelines struggle, post-trained ViT-H achieved an 80.0% success rate offline and 63.8% in online autoregressive mode. Comparing with the pre-trained checkpoint without post-training ("w/o PT"), post-training boosted success from 74.8% to 80.0% offline, and from 49.6% to 63.8% online.

### 4.2 Dissecting DPO Post-Training
Ablation studies shed light on why DPO works. On reward design, adding global trajectory rewards from the privileged tracker alongside local pose rewards from the deployable tracker yielded notable gains (61.5% to 63.8% online). On parameter updates, fine-tuning only the top 8 layers of the 16-layer Transformer backbone provided the most stable and highest performance.

### 4.3 Scaling Laws and Generalization across Trackers
Scaling model parameters from 49.9M to 224.7M led to monotonic improvements in tracking success. Similar scaling behavior held across pre-training and post-training data volumes. Crucially, the policy generalized well: when evaluated with three external trackers not used during DPO (Humanoid-GPT, ScaleBFM, HoloMotion), tracking success improved and tracking errors dropped. This confirms that the generator did not simply overfit to the training tracker's idiosyncrasies, but learned fundamentally executable motions.

sections.heading: Trackers are both motion executors and supervisors for generation
sections.summary: ViT-H eliminates conventional pipeline bottlenecks through direct video-to-humanoid generation and tracking feedback learning. Using trackers not merely as executors but as supervisory evaluators during post-training offers a compelling blueprint for future humanoid foundation models.
sections.details:
This study fundamentally rethinks how humanoid robots learn from video. Rather than decoupling human motion reconstruction from retargeting, ViT-H models reference motions directly in the robot's joint space using a diffusion model. Using a pre-trained whole-body tracker as a critic to post-train the generator via DPO represents a significant breakthrough.

The authors conclude with an insightful observation: as whole-body tracking policies mature, they will serve not only as motion executors, but also as supervisors that guide and refine generative motion models—a perspective with broad implications for humanoid foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-world teleoperation details and dataset curation
sections.summary: The appendix details the experimental setup for sub-400 ms real-world teleoperation on the Unitree G1, along with the retargeting and filtering procedures used to prepare large-scale training data.
sections.details:
### Real-World Teleoperation Setup
In real-robot experiments, an Intel RealSense D455 camera mounted at a height of 1.2 m captures a human operator. Combining the autoregressive generator $\pi_{\text{gen}}^{\text{ar}}$ with the tracker achieves sub-400 ms latency from visual input to robot joint actuation, enabling the Unitree G1 to smoothly step and move its arms in response to the operator's whole-body motions.

### Curation for Large-Scale Training Data
Pre-training leverages roughly 384 hours of motion data. When mapping human motion datasets to the Unitree G1, running standard inverse-kinematics-based GMR often fails because initial frame errors propagate through the sequence. The authors improved this by sampling multiple random seeds and selecting the longest valid trajectory. Stringent data cleaning also filtered out sequences with excessive root jerk, foot floating, or self-penetration exceeding 2 cm over more than 5% of frames, providing a clean training foundation.

captions.F3: Real-world video teleoperation setup presented in the appendix. A RealSense D455 camera mounted on a stand captures the operator's whole body, while the adjacent Unitree G1 replicates the observed behavior in real time from the streaming video.

takeaways: Directly generating robot motions from video in an end-to-end manner prevents error accumulation and delivers higher motion quality than multi-stage pipelines (reconstruction -> retargeting -> tracking).

Feeding downstream tracking success and failure back into the generator via DPO enables self-improvement toward physically executable motions, even using uncurated internet videos without 3D ground truth.
Incorporating global offset feedback from a privileged tracker into DPO rewards stabilizes overall global trajectory tracking in addition to local pose fidelity.
Improvements from tracking feedback generalize to unseen tracking policies, demonstrating that the generator learns morphology-aligned physical executability rather than tracker-specific quirks.
limitations: Dexterous hand poses and finger manipulation are not modeled, precluding fine-grained object grasping tasks.
Due to compute and data constraints, scaling behavior was not tested beyond the current maximum model size (around 225M parameters) and dataset scale.
Root translational tracking accuracy in online autoregressive mode remains slightly lower than in offline mode, which has access to the complete future video context.
